title: Joint probability
summary: A joint probability assigns mass to pairs. The same 2 by 2 table yields both marginals, by adding, and conditionals, by the multiplication rule.
intuition:
A joint probability describes two events, or two random variables, happening together. In a $2\times 2$ table each cell is a probability $P(X=x,Y=y)$, and the four cells add to 1. Nothing in the table is a conditional probability until you divide. The cell is the intersection, not the bar.

The table is used twice in this lesson, on purpose. The first pass adds a row or a column and calls the sum a marginal. The second pass divides a cell by the marginal just obtained and calls the quotient a conditional. The multiplication rule ties the two passes together: the cell equals the marginal times the conditional. If you know any two of the three numbers, the rule gives the third.

Independence is a property you can see in the table and can also fail to see. It holds when every cell equals the product of its row marginal and its column marginal. One cell that misses the product is enough dependence. A large cell is not evidence of independence, and it is not evidence that the two conditionals $P(X=x\mid Y=y)$ and $P(Y=y\mid X=x)$ are equal.

definitions.body: The probability $P(X=x,Y=y)$, or $P(A\cap B)$, of two specified outcomes happening together. In a finite table the joints are the cell entries.
The full assignment of joint probabilities to every pair $(x,y)$. For discrete variables the entries are nonnegative and sum to 1 over the whole table.
$P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)P(Y=y\mid X=x)=P(Y=y)P(X=x\mid Y=y)$, whenever the conditioning probability is positive. This recovers a joint cell from a marginal and a conditional.

formulas.name: Cell from a conditional
formulas.note: Requires $P(X=x)>0$. The symmetric form divides the other way: the cell is $P(Y=y)P(X=x\mid Y=y)$.

formulas.name: Marginals from the table
formulas.note: Add the row to get a marginal of $X$, and add the column to get a marginal of $Y$.

formulas.name: Independence in the table
formulas.note: Must hold for every pair $(x,y)$, not just for one cell. Otherwise $X$ and $Y$ are dependent.

properties: Every joint cell is nonnegative, and the sum of all the cells is 1.
Each cell is at most either marginal: $P(X=x,Y=y)\le \min\{P(X=x),P(Y=y)\}$.
The two conditionals from one cell generally differ, because they divide by different marginals.
Adding the conditional probabilities down a column does not give a marginal. Conditional probabilities in a fixed column, given that column's value, sum to 1.
If one cell fails the product test, the variables are dependent, even if another cell happens to match the product of its marginals.

examples.title: First pass: marginals from a 2 by 2 table
examples.prompt: A joint distribution on $X\in\{0,1\}$ and $Y\in\{0,1\}$ has $P(X=0,Y=0)=3/20$, $P(X=0,Y=1)=1/4$, $P(X=1,Y=0)=1/5$, and $P(X=1,Y=1)=2/5$. Recover the marginals, and test independence at the cell $(0,0)$.
steps: Write the cells over 20: $3/20$, $5/20$, $4/20$, and $8/20$. They sum to $20/20=1$, so the table is a joint distribution.
The independence product at $(0,0)$ is $(2/5)(7/20)=7/50=14/100$. The cell is $3/20=15/100$. Because $15/100\neq 14/100$, $X$ and $Y$ are not independent.
examples.answer: The marginals are $P(X=0)=2/5$, $P(X=1)=3/5$, $P(Y=0)=7/20$, and $P(Y=1)=13/20$. The variables are dependent.

examples.title: Second pass: the same table, by the multiplication rule
examples.prompt: Using the same cells $3/20$, $1/4$, $1/5$, and $2/5$, compute $P(Y=1\mid X=1)$ and $P(X=1\mid Y=1)$, and recover the cell $P(X=1,Y=1)$ from the first of those conditionals.
steps: The cell $P(X=1,Y=1)=2/5=8/20$, the row marginal is $P(X=1)=3/5=12/20$, and the column marginal is $P(Y=1)=13/20$.
Divide by the row: $P(Y=1\mid X=1)=(8/20)/(12/20)=8/12=2/3$. Divide by the column: $P(X=1\mid Y=1)=(8/20)/(13/20)=8/13$. These are not equal.
The multiplication rule returns the cell: $P(X=1)P(Y=1\mid X=1)=(3/5)(2/3)=2/5$, which is the original entry.
examples.answer: $P(Y=1\mid X=1)=2/3$ and $P(X=1\mid Y=1)=8/13$. Their common cell is $2/5$, recovered as $(3/5)(2/3)$.

traps: Reading a cell of the joint table as a conditional probability. The cell $2/5$ becomes $2/3$ only after dividing by $P(X=1)$.
Multiplying marginals to fill a cell when the table has not passed the independence test. In this table $(2/5)(7/20)$ misses $3/20$.
Adding conditional probabilities and calling the sum a marginal. Conditionals given the same event already sum to 1.
Equating $P(X=x\mid Y=y)$ with $P(Y=y\mid X=x)$. On this table those numbers are $8/13$ and $2/3$.
python:
from fractions import Fraction
cells = [Fraction(3, 20), Fraction(1, 4), Fraction(1, 5), Fraction(2, 5)]
assert sum(cells) == 1
px1 = cells[2] + cells[3]
py1 = cells[1] + cells[3]
assert px1 == Fraction(3, 5)
assert py1 == Fraction(13, 20)
assert cells[3] / px1 == Fraction(2, 3)
assert cells[3] / py1 == Fraction(8, 13)
assert Fraction(2, 5) * Fraction(7, 20) != Fraction(3, 20)
gap = Fraction(3, 5) * Fraction(7, 10) - Fraction(2, 5)
assert gap == Fraction(1, 50)
print(float(cells[3] / px1), float(gap))

questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $3/5$.

Add the two cells in the row $X=1$: $1/5+2/5=3/5$. Option B is a single cell, $P(X=1,Y=1)$. Option C is $P(Y=1)=3/10+2/5=7/10$, the other marginal.

questions.stem: A joint table has $P(X=0,Y=0)=1/10$, $P(X=0,Y=1)=3/10$, $P(X=1,Y=0)=1/5$, and $P(X=1,Y=1)=2/5$. Then $P(Y=1\mid X=0)$ equals
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $3/4$.

The row marginal is $P(X=0)=1/10+3/10=2/5$. Divide the cell by that marginal: $(3/10)/(2/5)=(3/10)\times(5/2)=3/4$. Option B is the other conditional $P(X=0\mid Y=1)=(3/10)/(7/10)=3/7$. Option C is the joint cell before dividing.

questions.stem: A joint table has cells $P(X=0,Y=0)=1/10$, $P(X=0,Y=1)=3/10$, $P(X=1,Y=0)=1/5$, and $P(X=1,Y=1)=2/5$. Which of the following are true?
options: The four joint cells sum to 1.
Adding the two cells in a row produces a marginal probability of $X$.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and D**.

The cells are $1/10+3/10+2/10+4/10=1$. The multiplication rule gives $P(X=1,Y=1)=P(X=1)P(Y=1\mid X=1)$ whenever $P(X=1)>0$, which it is: both sides equal $2/5$. Adding a row is the marginal. C fails because $P(X=1)P(Y=1)=(3/5)(7/10)=21/50$, while the cell is $2/5=20/50$.

The answer is **3**.

The cell is already the joint probability $p=3/10$, so $10p=3$. It is not the conditional $P(Y=1\mid X=0)=3/4$, and it is not the row marginal $2/5$.

The answer is **2**.

$P(X=1)=3/5$ and $P(Y=1)=7/10$, so the product is $21/50$. The joint cell is $2/5=20/50$. The positive difference is $1/50$, and $100$ times that difference is 2. A zero difference would have meant this cell matched independence.
